transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because... I guess I just can’t seem to stop launching all these projects. It's constant right now. I'm drawing up massive new work plans, mapping out all these certification schedules, completely upgrading my home network... which, by the way, I decided to rip out the drywall to run Cat6a cable everywhere. Future-proofing, you know? I even started messaging this guy Dave, an old contact from a job I had back in 2014, to ask him about his router setup. Dave always bought these really cheap network switches, which never made sense to me on an IT manager's salary, but he drove this terrible beat-up Honda too, so maybe he was just cheap. 

But anyway, I just start all these things—the messages to old contacts, the work plans—and it gets so intense that I just blow right past normal limits. I don't even sleep or stop to eat, I just keep building and planning until my wife or my director at work finally has to step in and physically stop me. Which is frustrating because my director doesn't even understand half the system architecture I'm proposing, but he's the one telling me to put the brakes on.
Do you often act on these plans without thinking them through?

I don't really know if I do or not... I mean, to me, I feel like I'm thinking them through completely. It all makes perfect sense in my head, it's just pure logic. Like, A leads to B, B leads to C. Which is exactly what I was trying to explain to my director about the new database architecture. He wants to keep using this legacy software that is basically a dinosaur. 

Speaking of which, I was actually watching this documentary at like 3 AM about the asteroid that wiped out the dinosaurs, and they were talking about the iridium layer in the earth's crust. It's fascinating how a single impact just leaves this permanent global footprint in the rock. I actually have a footprint cast from when I was a baby, my mom just found it in her attic last month when she was clearing out boxes. She has so many boxes up there, mostly old clothes she thinks will come back into style. I keep telling her that those massive shoulder pads from 1988 are never coming back, but she just won't listen, she just hoards it all. 

But... wait, what were you asking me about the plans?
Do you often find yourself saying things or acting without considering the consequences?

I guess... I mean, consequences? Not really, no. Because when I'm doing it, it's the absolute right thing to do. Like ripping out the drywall—my wife was furious, saying I didn't think about the dust or the cost of patching it. But I did think about it! I just knew the network speeds would justify it. 

Which reminds me, the drywall guy I called to give an estimate on fixing it? He showed up in this truck that had the most incredible custom paint job. It was this deep, metallic cherry red, almost like the color of those candied apples you get at the state fair. We used to go to the state fair every summer when I was a kid. My dad would always try to win one of those giant stuffed bears by throwing darts at balloons, but the darts are always dull, you know? It's a total scam. The physics of it just don't work out unless you throw it with an unreasonable amount of force. Force equals mass times acceleration, right? Basic physics. I actually took AP Physics in high school, Mr. Henderson was the teacher. He had this weird habit of clicking his pen exactly three times before he answered any question. Click, click, click. 

Anyway... consequences. Yeah, I don't really think I'm ignoring consequences, I just see the bigger picture that other people are missing.
Do you feel like you're in control of when you start and stop these projects?

In control? No, I wouldn't say I'm in control of it. It's more like a motor that just turns on and I have to move. Like, I’ll pace around the house with my laptop, then I'll go reorganize the garage, then I'm back inside rewriting all my project boards. I feel physically uncomfortable if I try to just sit down and, I don't know, watch a show with my wife. 

We tried watching that new sci-fi show the other night, the one about the colony on Mars? But the science in it was so incredibly flawed. They had them walking around in normal gravity, which makes zero sense because Martian gravity is only about 38% of Earth's. I actually did a whole presentation on terraforming Mars for my astronomy elective in college. Professor Davis gave me an A-minus because he said my timeline was "too aggressive." Which is hilarious, considering Elon Musk is basically proposing the exact same timeline now. Musk is an interesting guy, right? I mean, the whole electric car thing completely disrupted the automotive industry. My neighbor just bought one of those electric trucks, and it is completely silent. It's almost dangerous, honestly. He backed out of his driveway yesterday and I didn't even hear him coming while I was walking the dog. 

My dog is a Golden Retriever, by the way. Buster. He's terrified of the vacuum cleaner, which is a Dyson. I took the Dyson apart last month because the suction was failing, and the internal cyclone mechanism is actually a brilliant piece of engineering... but yeah, sitting still? I just can't do it right now. The motor just keeps running.
Are these projects and activities causing problems for you at work or in your relationships?

Problems? I mean, yeah, I guess you could say that. At work, they actually put me on administrative leave after the whole database migration thing failed. Which is ridiculous, because if they had just given me another 48 hours, I could have patched the routing errors. But no, HR got involved, and now I'm on "leave." 

HR departments are so bureaucratic anyway. It's like they exist just to generate paperwork. I remember my first job out of college, the HR lady made me fill out the same tax form three times because she kept losing it. She used these bright pink sticky notes for everything. I actually hate the color pink. When my wife and I were painting our guest room, she wanted this color called "Desert Rose," which is basically just dusty pink. We compromised on a sage green, which is much more calming. Green is supposed to reduce eye strain, which is why older computer terminals used green text on black screens. I actually have an original IBM terminal in the basement that I bought off eBay. The shipping cost more than the terminal itself because those things weigh a ton. 

But yeah, my wife... she's been really stressed. She's basically had to take over all the finances because of my spending on the server parts, and she gets so mad when I'm working at 4 AM. Every conversation we have lately just turns into this massive argument. 

And I haven't even been doing my normal stuff. Like, I used to play piano for the worship team at our church, but I had to step back because I just can't commit to showing up for rehearsals right now. Music theory is fascinating, though. The way chords are constructed based on mathematical intervals... it's just math translated into sound. Bach was basically a mathematician if you really analyze his fugues. The counterpoint is so precise. I tried explaining that to my climbing partner, Dave, but he wasn't really getting it. I haven't been rock climbing with him in weeks, either. Or doing my mentoring program. I just... I can't reliably show up for any of it right now. There's just too much to do.
Do you feel like your current way of thinking and acting is causing you a lot of distress?

Distress? I don't... I mean, I guess I'm not really sure if I'd call it distress. It's more like I just have so much energy and there's so much happening, you know? But my wife is definitely distressed. She's been crying a lot, which makes me feel bad, but I just don't have the time to sit and talk about feelings when the servers need to be calibrated. 

Calibrating servers is actually a lot like tuning a piano, if you think about it. You have to get the frequencies just right so everything resonates perfectly. I used to tune my own piano when I was playing for the church. I bought this professional tuning hammer and a set of rubber mutes. The guy at the music store tried to talk me out of it, said it takes years of apprenticeship to learn how to tune a piano properly. But it's really just physics and acoustics. It's like how they tune the engines in Formula One cars. Have you ever watched F1? The engineering in those cars is unbelievable. They can change all four tires in under two seconds. Two seconds! I timed myself once trying to change a flat tire on my Honda Civic, and it took me twenty-four minutes. And that was with a power drill. 

Honda makes incredibly reliable engines, though. They started out making motorized bicycles after World War II. The founder, Soichiro Honda, he was a real visionary. He actually started out making piston rings for Toyota, but they rejected his first batch because the quality wasn't good enough. So he went back to school, figured out the metallurgy, and tried again. Metallurgy is fascinating. The way carbon bonds with iron to make steel... 

But wait, what were you asking? Oh, distress. Yeah, I don't know if I'm distressed. I just feel like I'm running out of time to get everything done.
Have you lost any important relationships or jobs because of your behavior or projects?

Well, like I was saying a minute ago, I haven't technically been fired, but being put on administrative leave after that migration failed feels pretty close. It's basically corporate purgatory. Purgatory is a fascinating concept, actually. Dante's Purgatorio is structurally much more complex than Inferno, even though everyone only ever reads Inferno in high school. We had to read it in 10th grade, and my English teacher, Mr. Harrison, used to spit a little when he talked. He had this massive collection of sweater vests. I think he owned one in every conceivable color. Color theory is really interesting when you get into it, actually. Like how magenta doesn't actually exist on the light spectrum, your brain just makes it up to bridge the gap between red and violet. 

But, uh, relationships... I mean, my wife hasn't left me, but like I mentioned, she had to completely step in and take over the spending, and she's so angry about me working late into the night. Every conversation we have just turns into a massive argument now. And I guess I haven't formally lost my friends, but I completely pulled away from playing music at church, and I stopped climbing with Dave, and I dropped my mentoring program. I just can't reliably follow through or show up for any of that right now. Showing up is 80 percent of life, right? That's the quote. Quotes get misattributed on the internet all the time, though. Abraham Lincoln has like a thousand fake quotes attributed to him online. The internet has really destroyed our ability to verify primary sources. It's an archival nightmare, honestly, the way data degrades over time...
Do you have periods where you feel completely normal and not like you're constantly starting new projects and activities?

Normal? I mean, yeah, I guess so. There are definitely times when I'm not... you know, not building servers or trying to fix everything all at once. Like, there have been these stretches, maybe a few weeks at a time, where things are just kind of flat. I'm not super energized, but I'm not depressed either. Just... calm, I guess. 

But even then, during those calm periods, I still... I still know about the Teams statuses. Like, the coded warnings are still there. You know, when someone goes from "Available" to "Away" exactly three minutes after a meeting starts? It's a signal. Signals are everywhere if you know how to look for them. It's like semaphore, you know? The flag signals they use in the Navy. My grandfather was in the Navy. He served on a destroyer in the Pacific. He used to tell me stories about how they'd communicate between ships using flashing lights when they had to maintain radio silence. Radio silence is actually really hard to achieve because everything emits some kind of electromagnetic frequency. Even your brain. That's how EEGs work. 

And, um, even during those flat weeks, I still hear things sometimes. Just brief comments, you know? Like someone whispering something when the house is completely empty. It's weird because the acoustics in our house shouldn't allow for that kind of sound travel. We have plaster walls, not drywall. Plaster is way denser. It's terrible for Wi-Fi signals, actually. I had to set up a mesh network just to get a decent connection in the kitchen. Mesh networks are brilliant because they use multiple nodes to create a single, seamless network. It's basically a localized intranet. Intranets used to be huge in the 90s before everyone just moved everything to the cloud. The "cloud" is such a stupid term, though. It's just someone else's computer. 

But yeah, to answer your question, there are periods where I'm not constantly starting new projects, but the other stuff... the warnings and the voices... that doesn't really go away.
Do you still talk a lot and have racing thoughts during those calm weeks you mentioned?

No, not really. During those flat weeks, I don't talk nearly as much. I'm pretty quiet, actually. But the racing thoughts... those don't always stop. Even when I'm not doing a million things, my thoughts can move so fast that one idea just opens ten more tabs in my head. Like, I'll be typing an email, and by the time I'm halfway through a sentence, I'm already three solutions ahead and completely losing the original point. 

It's exactly like how web browsers manage memory. Chrome is notorious for being a memory hog, especially if you have a lot of tabs open. Each tab runs as a separate process, which is great for stability—if one tab crashes, the whole browser doesn't go down—but it just eats up your RAM. RAM is so cheap now, though. I remember when upgrading to 16 megabytes of RAM was a huge deal. Megabytes! Now my phone has 12 gigabytes. The miniaturization of transistors is incredible. Moore's Law said the number of transistors on a microchip doubles about every two years, but we're starting to hit the physical limits of silicon now. They're looking into quantum computing, which uses qubits instead of binary bits. Qubits can exist in multiple states at once thanks to superposition. Superposition is a wild concept. It's like Schrödinger's cat, you know? The cat is both alive and dead until you open the box. 

I've never really liked cats, to be honest. They're too unpredictable. Dogs are much easier to read. Their body language is so straightforward. But yeah, the fast thoughts... they happen even when I'm just sitting quietly.
Do you talk excessively during those calm weeks you mentioned?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I just said I'm pretty quiet during those weeks, right? So, no, not excessive talking. It's more of an internal noise. But actually, talking excessively is really subjective anyway. What's excessive? Some people are just naturally verbose. My aunt Carol, for instance, she could talk to a brick wall for three hours and not even notice the wall wasn't responding. She used to call our house on Sunday evenings and my dad would just set the receiver on the counter and go make a sandwich, and she'd still be talking when he got back. Telephones used to have cords, you know? The long, coiled ones that would get all tangled up. I spent half my childhood untangling the phone cord in the kitchen. It's a topological problem, really, knot theory. Knot theory is a branch of topology that studies mathematical knots, which are different from everyday knots because the ends are joined together so it can't be undone. It has applications in quantum physics and understanding DNA replication. DNA is fascinating, how it just unzips itself to copy the code. But yeah, no, I don't talk a lot during those flat times.
Do you find yourself talking a lot even when you're not in the middle of one of these intense project periods?

I feel like we just covered this, but... no. No, I really don't talk a lot when I'm not doing all the projects. Like I said, I get pretty quiet. It's almost like my vocal cords just decide to take a break. Vocal cords are actually folds of tissue, not cords at all. It's a total misnomer. They vibrate when air passes through them from the lungs, and the pitch depends on how tightly they're stretched. It's basically the same principle as a guitar string. I tried to learn guitar in high school, but I couldn't get my fingers to stretch across the frets properly. I have these really short fingers. My mom has them too. She used to play the piano, though, which I never understood because you need a good reach for piano. She had this beautiful upright Yamaha. Yamaha makes everything, you know? Pianos, motorcycles, network routers... it's incredible how diversified they are. Diversification is key to a stable portfolio, they say. But yeah, no, I'm definitely not talking a lot when I'm in those flat periods.
Do you often dominate conversations when you're with friends or family, even when you're not working on a project?

Doc, I feel like you're just asking me the exact same thing in different ways now. No, I don't dominate conversations when I'm not in a project phase. Like I've been saying, I'm really quiet then. I usually just sit back and listen. 

Like, if I'm with my brother, he's the one doing all the talking. He runs a landscaping company, which is actually a lot more technical than people think. It's all about resource allocation and routing, kind of like network architecture. You have to route the water away from the foundation because water always follows the path of least resistance, just like an electrical current. That's exactly why we use routing protocols in IT to manage data traffic. BGP—Border Gateway Protocol—is basically the glue holding the entire internet together. It's fascinating because it was originally built on trust, which is just a terrible security model for the modern web. 

Remember when Facebook completely disappeared from the internet a couple of years ago? Someone botched a BGP update and they essentially deleted their own digital existence. They couldn't even get into their physical offices to fix it because the badge scanners were authenticated through the very servers that went down. It's a classic example of why you never tie physical access control entirely to a centralized logical network without a mechanical fail-safe. You always need a physical key backup. Failsafes are just critical in any system design. 

But anyway, yeah, when I'm with family during those slow weeks, I'm definitely not the one doing all the talking. I just let them run the conversation.
Do you often find yourself easily distracted by things around you?

Oh, constantly. Especially when I'm wired up and working on things. It's like my brain has no filter for background noise. If a phone buzzes, or a fan clicks, or someone just walks past my office door, my attention snaps right to it and I’ll completely abandon whatever report or support ticket I was supposed to finish. 

Speaking of fans, the HVAC system in our office building is an absolute nightmare. It's this ancient pneumatic system from the 80s. They use compressed air to control the thermostats instead of digital sensors, which is just absurdly inefficient. Compressed air systems leak all the time, and when the pressure drops, the compressor has to kick in, and it makes this horrible humming noise. It's the exact same kind of air compressor you'd use for pneumatic tools in an auto shop. 

I took my car to the shop last week because the check engine light came on. Turns out it was just a faulty O2 sensor. The mechanic tried to charge me four hundred dollars for it, but the part itself is only like fifty bucks online. You can literally just unscrew it with a special socket wrench. Mechanics always upcharge on parts, it's a huge markup industry. It's basically highway robbery, honestly. You have to do your own research or they just take you to the cleaners. 

But yeah, what were we talking about? Oh, right, getting distracted. Yeah, any little noise like that fan clicking and I'm totally derailed from my tickets.
Is your difficulty with staying focused and being easily distracted something that happens all the time, or is it mostly when you're in the middle of one of these intense project periods?

It's definitely mostly when I'm in those intense project periods. When I'm wired up like that, I just can't filter anything out. Like I said, if a phone buzzes, or a fan clicks, or someone just walks past my office door, my attention just snaps right to it, and I'll completely abandon whatever report or ticket I was supposed to finish. 

Tickets are the absolute worst part of my job, by the way. The ticketing system we use is Jira, and it's just bloated. Everyone thinks they need to customize every single workflow, and before you know it, you have thirty different required fields just to log a password reset. Passwords are such an outdated security model anyway. We should all be moving to biometric authentication or hardware security keys, like YubiKeys. I bought a YubiKey for my personal accounts, and it's amazing. It uses near-field communication, NFC, so you just tap it on your phone. NFC is the same tech they use for contactless payments, which really took off during the pandemic. I remember reading that cash usage dropped by something like forty percent in 2020 because everyone was afraid of germs on the bills. Paper money is actually mostly cotton and linen, not paper, which is why it survives going through the washing machine. I accidentally washed a twenty-dollar bill last week when I was doing laundry. I hate doing laundry, the folding takes forever. 

But yeah, when I'm in those high-energy phases, that's when the distraction is just off the charts. If I'm not in a project phase, I can usually focus well enough.
Is your difficulty with staying focused something that you experience even when you're not working on any projects?

Doc, I feel like we're going in circles here. No, like I just said, it's really not an issue when I'm not in one of those high-energy project phases. I can focus fine then. It's only when I'm all wired up that every little thing gets me. Like I was just telling you, if a phone buzzes, or that stupid fan clicks, or somebody just walks past my office door, my brain latches right onto it and I'll completely drop whatever ticket or report I'm supposed to be doing. 

Speaking of the office door, whoever invented open-concept offices should honestly be put in jail. They took away my actual solid wood door two years ago when they remodeled the floor. Now it's all glass partitions. Glass is absolutely terrible for acoustics. Sound waves just bounce right off it with zero absorption. You really need soft materials to absorb sound, like acoustic foam. I bought some of those foam panels for my home setup, the ones that look like egg cartons. Real egg cartons don't actually work for soundproofing, by the way, that's a total myth. They don't have the mass to block sound, they just diffuse it a little bit. Kind of like how a prism diffuses light. Pink Floyd had that prism on the Dark Side of the Moon cover. Great album, but vinyl is so ridiculously expensive now. Everyone says vinyl sounds warmer, but digitally lossless audio is technically superior. It's just math, you can't argue with the sample rate. 

But yeah, to answer your question, no, the distraction thing is really just when I'm in one of those intense project modes. Otherwise I'm fine.
Is your difficulty with staying focused something that you experience even when you're not working on any projects or feeling highly energetic?

Doc, are you messing with me? I feel like I'm taking a crazy pill here, you literally just asked me that. Like I keep saying, no. When I'm not energetic, my focus is completely fine. It's only when my brain is in overdrive that the distractibility hits. That's when—like I've told you three times now—a buzzing phone, a clicking fan, or some guy walking past my door makes me completely abandon my tickets and reports. 

I actually had to buy active noise-canceling headphones just to survive those phases at work. I got the Sony ones. The tech in them is actually brilliant—they use external microphones to listen to the room, and then play an inverted sound wave into your ear to cancel the noise out. Destructive interference, it's called. They use the exact same physics for stealth technology on military submarines. Submarines are wild, honestly. The pressure they have to withstand is insane. Did you know if a sub hull breaches at extreme depths, the air inside compresses so fast it actually ignites? It's called the diesel effect. It's the exact same way a diesel engine in a car works. There are no spark plugs, just pure compression heating the fuel until it combusts. Diesel engines last way longer than gas ones because of how overbuilt they have to be to handle that pressure. My buddy has a Volkswagen TDI with like three hundred thousand miles on it and it still runs like a top. The emissions scandal with VW was a huge mess, though. They wrote code into the car's computer specifically to cheat the emissions testing machines. As an IT guy, I kind of have to respect the cleverness of the code, even if it was highly illegal. 

But anyway... yeah. To answer your question again, no, I only lose focus and drop my work like that when I'm highly energetic.
Is your difficulty with staying focused something that you experience even when you're feeling calm and not working on any projects?

Okay, seriously, is there a hidden camera in here? Are you testing my patience, or is this some kind of memory test? I feel like I'm stuck in Groundhog Day. For the fourth time, doc, no. When I am calm, my focus is perfectly fine. I only get distracted when my brain is running at a million miles an hour. That is when—and I really don't know how else to phrase this for you—a phone buzzing, a fan clicking, or literally just someone walking past my office door makes me completely drop the ticket or report I'm working on. 

Speaking of Groundhog Day, Bill Murray actually got bitten by the groundhog on set. Twice, I think. He had to get rabies shots. Rabies is a terrifying virus, honestly. By the time you show symptoms, it's basically one hundred percent fatal. It travels straight up your nervous system to your brain. Viruses are fascinating though. Computer viruses are modeled exactly after biological ones, which is why we call them that. The first computer virus was called the Creeper program back in the early seventies on ARPANET. It just displayed a message saying "I'm the creeper, catch me if you can." ARPANET was funded by the Department of Defense, so the military basically invented the internet, and now we use it to watch cat videos and argue with strangers on Reddit. 

Cats actually domesticated themselves, you know. They just started hanging around human grain silos to eat the mice, and humans were like, "cool, stay." Ancient Egyptians literally worshipped them. Did you know the pyramids were built by paid laborers, not slaves? That's a huge historical misconception. They even found ancient payroll records detailing their daily rations of beer and bread. Fermentation is probably one of the oldest human technologies. I tried brewing my own beer in my garage a few years ago, but keeping the temperature exactly right during the fermentation process is incredibly tedious. 

But anyway, yeah. If I'm calm, I'm focused. I only drop my work when I'm wired. Are we clear on that now?
Is your difficulty with staying focused something that you experience even when you're not feeling highly energetic and not working on any projects?

Are you... are you actually doing a bit right now? Is this a joke? Because I'm starting to feel really disrespected here. I have answered this exact same question, phrased slightly differently, four times now. Four! 

No. For the love of God, no. If I am not highly energetic, if I am not in a project phase, I am completely fine. My focus is normal. It is only—only—when I am totally wired that I get distracted. That is when, like I have been trying to tell you, a phone buzzing, a fan clicking, or someone walking past my office door makes my attention snap right to it, and I'll abandon whatever report or ticket I was supposed to finish. 

Speaking of finishing things, the completion rate for massive open online courses, those MOOCs, is abysmal. It's like less than ten percent. People sign up for these free Harvard or MIT coding classes and just never finish them. I think it's because there's no financial skin in the game. If you don't pay for it, you don't value it. It's basic behavioral economics. Kahneman and Tversky won a Nobel prize for that stuff. Well, Kahneman did, Tversky died before he could get it, and they don't award Nobels posthumously. Which is kind of unfair if you ask me. Rosalind Franklin got totally screwed out of the Nobel for discovering the structure of DNA because she died, and Watson and Crick just took all the credit. The history of science is full of stolen credit. Thomas Edison was basically just a patent troll who stole ideas from Tesla. Tesla actually wanted to provide free wireless electricity to the whole world, but J.P. Morgan pulled his funding because you can't put a meter on free energy. Corporate greed has literally held back human progress by decades. Imagine if we had free wireless power right now, we wouldn't even need lithium-ion batteries. 

Anyway. I really hope you wrote it down this time. I only lose focus when I'm wired. Please tell me we can move on.
Is your mind often preoccupied with thoughts, even when you're not working on any projects or feeling highly energetic?

Okay, wow, a different question. Thank you. I appreciate the variety. 

Um, preoccupied? Yeah, I mean, my thoughts can move so fast that one idea just opens ten more tabs in my head. By the time I’m typing an email, I’m already three solutions ahead and totally losing the original point of what I was trying to say. 

Speaking of tabs, Google Chrome is an absolute nightmare for RAM usage. I tell my team this all the time. It isolates every single tab into its own separate process so if one crashes, the whole browser doesn't go down. Which is smart architecture, sure, but it eats up memory like crazy. That's why you need at least sixteen gigs of RAM on a machine these days just to do basic office work. RAM prices actually spiked a few years ago because of a fire at a semiconductor plant in Taiwan, plus a power outage at a Samsung factory. It's crazy how fragile the global supply chain really is. It's just like during the pandemic when you couldn't get a graphics card to save your life because crypto miners were buying them all up by the pallet using automated bot scripts. 

Crypto is basically just a giant Ponzi scheme anyway, backed by nothing but wasted electricity. The carbon footprint of Bitcoin alone is larger than some entire countries, like Argentina or New Zealand. New Zealand is where they filmed Lord of the Rings, obviously. The forced perspective camera tricks Peter Jackson used to make the hobbits look small next to Gandalf are incredible. They didn't even use CGI for a lot of it, just math and precise camera angles. Practical effects always hold up better than CGI. If you look at Jurassic Park from the nineties, the animatronic T-Rex looks way more realistic than the dinosaurs in the new movies. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my mind being preoccupied. Yeah, the ten tabs thing. It just goes way too fast sometimes.
Do you often have difficulty organizing tasks and activities, even when you're not feeling highly energetic or working on a project?

Difficulty organizing? No, not at all. I mean, I'm an information systems manager. Organizing tasks and workflows is literally what they pay me to do. As long as I'm just at my normal baseline, not totally wired or obsessed with some new project, my organization is completely fine. I live and die by my calendar and project boards. 

We use Jira for everything at work. Honestly, Jira can be an absolute beast to configure on the backend, but once you get the sprint workflows set up, it's pretty seamless. It's made by Atlassian, which is an Australian company. The founders started it with just a credit card and now they're billionaires. Australia is such a wild place, though. Almost everything there evolved completely in isolation so it's all either venomous or massive. Did you know the Australian government actually fought a war against emus in the 1930s? It's called the Great Emu War. They literally deployed the military with Lewis machine guns to cull the emu population because the birds were destroying all the wheat crops. But the emus were too fast and their feathers were so thick that the bullets barely did anything, so the military basically surrendered. Imagine losing a war to giant flightless birds. 

But I guess birds are technically theropod dinosaurs, so maybe it makes sense. It's crazy to think about time scales like that. Like, the Tyrannosaurus Rex lived closer in history to humans than it did to the Stegosaurus. Most people don't realize that. Just like Cleopatra lived closer to the invention of the iPhone than to the building of the pyramids. Which I was just talking about, the pyramids. 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Organizing tasks? Right, yeah. No, I don't have any trouble with that. Unless my energy is through the roof, I'm perfectly organized.

doctor.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

target_item.name: Increased_Goal_Activity
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can’t seem to stop launching projects—work plans, certification schedules, home network upgrades, messages to old contacts—and it gets so intense that I blow past normal limits until my wife or my director has to step in.

patient.answer:
Well, I came in because... I guess I just can’t seem to stop launching all these projects. It's constant right now. I'm drawing up massive new work plans, mapping out all these certification schedules, completely upgrading my home network... which, by the way, I decided to rip out the drywall to run Cat6a cable everywhere. ARPANET was funded by the Department of Defense, so the military basically invented the internet, and now we use it to watch cat videos and argue with strangers on Reddit. 

Cats actually domesticated themselves, you know. They just started hanging around human grain silos to eat the mice, and humans were like, "cool, stay." Ancient Egyptians literally worshipped them. Did you know the pyramids were built by paid laborers, not slaves? That's a huge historical misconception. They even found ancient payroll records detailing their daily rations of beer and bread. Fermentation is probably one of the oldest human technologies. I tried brewing my own beer in my garage a few years ago, but keeping the temperature exactly right during the fermentation process is incredibly tedious. 

But anyway, yeah. If I'm calm, I'm focused. I only drop my work when I'm wired. Are we clear on that now?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's distractibility is a persistent trait or only occurs during intense project periods
doctor.question: Is your difficulty with staying focused something that you experience even when you're not feeling highly energetic and not working on any projects?

target_item.name: Manic_Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: If a phone buzzes, a fan clicks, or someone walks past my office door, my attention snaps to it and I’ll abandon whatever report or ticket I was supposed to finish.
target_item.reason: The doctor is again asking about my difficulty staying focused and whether it happens outside of my highly energetic phases, which relates to manic distractibility.

patient.answer:
Are you... are you actually doing a bit right now? Is this a joke? Because I'm starting to feel really disrespected here. I have answered this exact same question, phrased slightly differently, four times now. Four! 

No. For the love of God, no. If I am not highly energetic, if I am not in a project phase, I am completely fine. My focus is normal. It is only—only—when I am totally wired that I get distracted. That is when, like I have been trying to tell you, a phone buzzing, a fan clicking, or someone walking past my office door makes my attention snap right to it, and I'll abandon whatever report or ticket I was supposed to finish. 

Speaking of finishing things, the completion rate for massive open online courses, those MOOCs, is abysmal. It's like less than ten percent. People sign up for these free Harvard or MIT coding classes and just never finish them. I think it's because there's no financial skin in the game. If you don't pay for it, you don't value it. It's basic behavioral economics. Kahneman and Tversky won a Nobel prize for that stuff. Well, Kahneman did, Tversky died before he could get it, and they don't award Nobels posthumously. Which is kind of unfair if you ask me. Rosalind Franklin got totally screwed out of the Nobel for discovering the structure of DNA because she died, and Watson and Crick just took all the credit. The history of science is full of stolen credit. Thomas Edison was basically just a patent troll who stole ideas from Tesla. Tesla actually wanted to provide free wireless electricity to the whole world, but J.P. Morgan pulled his funding because you can't put a meter on free energy. Corporate greed has literally held back human progress by decades. Imagine if we had free wireless power right now, we wouldn't even need lithium-ion batteries. 

Anyway. I really hope you wrote it down this time. I only lose focus when I'm wired. Please tell me we can move on.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's distractibility is a persistent trait regardless of their energetic state
doctor.question: Is your mind often preoccupied with thoughts, even when you're not working on any projects or feeling highly energetic?

target_item.name: Racing_Thoughts
target_item.manifestation: My thoughts can move so fast that one idea opens ten more tabs in my head, and by the time I’m typing an email I’m already three solutions ahead and losing the original point.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if my mind is preoccupied with thoughts (racing thoughts) even when I am not highly energetic, which directly refers to the symptom of racing thoughts.

patient.answer:
Okay, wow, a different question. Thank you. I appreciate the variety. 

Um, preoccupied? Yeah, I mean, my thoughts can move so fast that one idea just opens ten more tabs in my head. By the time I’m typing an email, I’m already three solutions ahead and totally losing the original point of what I was trying to say. 

Speaking of tabs, Google Chrome is an absolute nightmare for RAM usage. I tell my team this all the time. It isolates every single tab into its own separate process so if one crashes, the whole browser doesn't go down. Which is smart architecture, sure, but it eats up memory like crazy. That's why you need at least sixteen gigs of RAM on a machine these days just to do basic office work. RAM prices actually spiked a few years ago because of a fire at a semiconductor plant in Taiwan, plus a power outage at a Samsung factory. It's crazy how fragile the global supply chain really is. It's just like during the pandemic when you couldn't get a graphics card to save your life because crypto miners were buying them all up by the pallet using automated bot scripts. 

Crypto is basically just a giant Ponzi scheme anyway, backed by nothing but wasted electricity. The carbon footprint of Bitcoin alone is larger than some entire countries, like Argentina or New Zealand. New Zealand is where they filmed Lord of the Rings, obviously. The forced perspective camera tricks Peter Jackson used to make the hobbits look small next to Gandalf are incredible. They didn't even use CGI for a lot of it, just math and precise camera angles. Practical effects always hold up better than CGI. If you look at Jurassic Park from the nineties, the animatronic T-Rex looks way more realistic than the dinosaurs in the new movies. 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, my mind being preoccupied. Yeah, the ten tabs thing. It just goes way too fast sometimes.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's symptoms meet the criteria for a specific attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) subtype
doctor.question: Do you often have difficulty organizing tasks and activities, even when you're not feeling highly energetic or working on a project?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty organizing tasks and activities, which is a symptom of ADHD. This is not covered in my symptom profile, which includes disorganized thinking/speech but not disorganized behavior or ADHD-related organizational difficulties.

patient.answer:
Difficulty organizing? No, not at all. I mean, I'm an information systems manager. Organizing tasks and workflows is literally what they pay me to do. As long as I'm just at my normal baseline, not totally wired or obsessed with some new project, my organization is completely fine. I live and die by my calendar and project boards. 

We use Jira for everything at work. Honestly, Jira can be an absolute beast to configure on the backend, but once you get the sprint workflows set up, it's pretty seamless. It's made by Atlassian, which is an Australian company. The founders started it with just a credit card and now they're billionaires. Australia is such a wild place, though. Almost everything there evolved completely in isolation so it's all either venomous or massive. Did you know the Australian government actually fought a war against emus in the 1930s? It's called the Great Emu War. They literally deployed the military with Lewis machine guns to cull the emu population because the birds were destroying all the wheat crops. But the emus were too fast and their feathers were so thick that the bullets barely did anything, so the military basically surrendered. Imagine losing a war to giant flightless birds. 

But I guess birds are technically theropod dinosaurs, so maybe it makes sense. It's crazy to think about time scales like that. Like, the Tyrannosaurus Rex lived closer in history to humans than it did to the Stegosaurus. Most people don't realize that. Just like Cleopatra lived closer to the invention of the iPhone than to the building of the pyramids. Which I was just talking about, the pyramids. 

Wait, sorry, what did you ask me? Organizing tasks? Right, yeah. No, I don't have any trouble with that. Unless my energy is through the roof, I'm perfectly organized.
